lesson.grammar_point: modal passive in contract language (shall be paid, is to be carried out, may be terminated)

listenings.text: I've been renting out apartments in Chicago for fifteen years, and the conversation I have most often is about the deposit. When a tenant moves out, they expect every cent back. When I look at the apartment, I see a list of repairs. The truth is usually somewhere in the middle. Normal wear and tear is my problem: faded paint, a carpet that has been walked on for three years, a door handle that has gotten loose. That is simply what happens when people live somewhere. Damage is different. A hole in the wall, a broken window, a burn on the kitchen counter: those are paid for by the tenant, and that money comes out of the deposit. My advice to anybody who rents is very simple. On the first day, walk through every room with your phone and take pictures of everything. Then send them to the landlord by email, so the date is recorded. Three years later, when we disagree about a scratch on the floor, those pictures will be worth more than any clause in the lease.

I have been drafting contracts for twenty-five years, and I still spend more time on one small word than on any other: shall. In a well-drafted contract, shall means one thing only: this party has a duty. The tenant shall pay the rent. The trouble starts when lawyers use the passive and forget to say who owes the duty. The premises shall be kept in good condition. By whom? The landlord, or the tenant? I once saw a dispute about a broken elevator last two years because of a sentence like that. So my rule is simple. Whenever you write a passive sentence in a contract, ask yourself whether the reader knows who has to act. If the answer is not obvious, add by and the name of the party, or rewrite the sentence in the active voice. The passive is not the enemy. It is useful when the action matters more than the person. But in a list of obligations, an obligation without an owner is an argument waiting to happen.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to keep something back that you would normally give
to correct a problem or a breach so that it no longer exists
to be legally responsible for something, and for paying for it
to pay somebody back for money they have spent
to be late with a payment that is already due
the person or company that rents a property from its owner
to rent all or part of a property you are renting to another person
the normal damage that happens when something is used over time

reading.rtitle: Office Lease -- Avenida Brigadeiro Faria Lima, 14th Floor: Key Clauses
paras: 4. Rent and Deposit. The Rent shall be paid monthly in advance, no later than the fifth business day of each month. A security deposit equal to three months' Rent is to be paid on signature and shall be held by the Lessor for the full term. If the Lessee is in arrears for more than thirty days, the Lessor may withhold the deposit to cover the amount owed.

7. Repairs and Maintenance. The Lessor shall be liable for structural repairs, including the roof, the facade and the central air-conditioning system. All other repairs are to be carried out by the Lessee, who shall bear the cost of keeping the premises in good condition. The Lessee shall not be held responsible for normal wear and tear.

9. Use and Subletting. The premises may be used only as offices. The Lessee may not sublet the premises, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of the Lessor, which shall not be unreasonably withheld. Any alterations must be approved in writing before work begins.

12. Breach and Termination. If either party fails to perform an obligation, it shall be given written notice and thirty days to remedy the breach. If the breach is not remedied within that period, the lease may be terminated by the other party. Any costs paid by the Lessee on the Lessor's behalf shall be reimbursed within fifteen days. Throughout the term, the Lessee shall be entitled to quiet enjoyment of the premises.

reading.prompt: What do these four clauses mainly do?
choices: They set the price of the office and explain how it will be adjusted each year, in line with inflation and the market.
They say who must do what, and what happens if one side fails.
They explain how the building was built.

items: If the central air-conditioning breaks, the Lessee has to pay for the repair.

Clause 9: consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.
A party that fails to perform an obligation gets a chance to fix it before the lease can be terminated.

The Lessor can keep the deposit if the rent is more than thirty days late.
Clause 4: if the Lessee is in arrears for more than thirty days, the Lessor may withhold the deposit.
